title: Mixed Conditionals
subtitle: Combine a past condition with a present result, or a present condition with a past result.
objectives: Combine a third-conditional "if" clause with a second-conditional result
Combine a second-conditional "if" clause with a third-conditional result
Recognize why real life often needs this mix, not a "pure" conditional

content.intro: Real regrets and hypotheticals often mix time frames — a past decision affecting the present, or a permanent truth affecting a past event. Mixed conditionals let you express that precisely.

rules.heading: a) Past condition → present result
rules.body:
If + past perfect, would + base verb. A past action (or its opposite) explains a present situation.

  • If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now. (I didn't study medicine, so I'm not a doctor now)

rules.heading: b) Present condition → past result
rules.body:
If + past simple, would have + past participle. A permanent truth/characteristic explains a past event.

  • If she weren't so shy, she would have spoken up at the meeting. (she is shy — a permanent trait — and that's why she didn't speak up, in the past)

examples: If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now.
If she weren't so shy, she would have spoken up at the meeting.
If he hadn't missed the flight, he would be here with us now.
If I were more organized, I wouldn't have forgotten the meeting.
If they had saved more money, they wouldn't be struggling now.
If you weren't so stubborn, you would have accepted their help.

commonMistakes.wrong: If I had studied medicine, I would have been a doctor now.
commonMistakes.right: If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now.
commonMistakes.why: "Now" signals a present result — use "would be," not "would have been."

commonMistakes.wrong: If she wasn't so shy, she would have spoken up.
commonMistakes.right: If she weren't so shy, she would have spoken up.
commonMistakes.why: The second-conditional "if" clause uses "were," not "was," for all subjects.

commonMistakes.wrong: If he hadn't missed the flight, he would have been here now.
commonMistakes.right: If he hadn't missed the flight, he would be here now.
commonMistakes.why: A present result ("now") needs "would be," not "would have been."

items.prompt: If I ___ (study) medicine, I ___ (be) a doctor now.
items.explanation: Past condition (didn't study) → present result — mixed conditional.

items.prompt: If she ___ (not/be) so shy, she ___ (speak up) at the meeting.
items.explanation: Present trait → past result — mixed conditional.

items.prompt: If he ___ (not/miss) the flight, he ___ (be) here with us now.
Which sentence correctly expresses "a past decision explains a present situation"?
options: If I had saved money, I would have bought a house.
If I had saved money, I would have a house now.
If I save money, I would have a house.
items.explanation: The past condition (didn't save) explains the present result (no house now) — mixed conditional.

items.prompt: Which sentence correctly expresses "a permanent trait explains a past event"?
options: If I am careless, I would have lost my keys.
If I were more careless, I will lose my keys.
If I weren't so careless, I wouldn't have lost my keys.
items.explanation: A permanent trait (carelessness) explains a past event (losing keys) — mixed conditional.

items.incorrect: If I had studied harder, I would have been fluent now.
answer: If I had studied harder, I would be fluent now.
items.explanation: "Now" needs the present result form, "would be," not "would have been."

items.incorrect: If you wasn't so stubborn, you would have accepted their help.
answer: If you weren't so stubborn, you would have accepted their help.
items.explanation: Use "weren't," not "wasn't," in the hypothetical "if" clause.

summary: Past condition → present result: If + past perfect, would + base verb.
Present condition → past result: If + past simple, would have + past participle.
Look for a time-clue word like "now" to tell you the result is present, not past.
